title: Nebuchadnezzar
lead: Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon (605–562 BC), who took Jerusalem, carried its people into exile and burned the Temple in 587/586 BC. The Bible remembers him both as God's instrument of judgment and as the proud king humbled by God, and later Jewish writers made him the type of every tyrant.

sections.b: Kings and Chronicles tell how Nebuchadnezzar made Jehoiakim his vassal, took Jehoiachin and the nobles to Babylon in 597 BC, and in his nineteenth year destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple (2 Kings 24:1–17; 2 Kings 25:1–21; 2 Chronicles 36:6–21). Jeremiah calls him God's "servant," to whom God has given the nations for a time, and urges Judah to submit to him (Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 27:6–8). Ezekiel sees him as God's sword against Tyre and Egypt (Ezekiel 26:7; Ezekiel 29:18–20). In Daniel he is the king who sets up a golden image and demands that all peoples worship it, then is humbled by madness until he acknowledges the Most High (Daniel 3:1–30; Daniel 4:28–37). Ezra remembers that God handed Jerusalem over to him because of Israel's sins (Ezra 5:12).
sections.refs: 2 Kings 24:1–17; 2 Kings 25:1–21; 2 Chronicles 36:6–21; Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 27:6–8; Ezekiel 26:7; Ezekiel 29:18–20; Daniel 3:1–30; Daniel 4:28–37; Ezra 5:12

sections.h: Servant of God or enemy of God?
sections.b: The Bible holds two pictures of the same king. In Jeremiah and Ezekiel he is the tool God uses to judge his people, and resisting him is resisting God (Jeremiah 27:8; Jeremiah 38:17–18). In Daniel he is the proud ruler who must learn that "the Most High rules over the kingdom of men" (Daniel 4:17). Later Jewish writers, freed from the need to explain the exile, kept mostly the second picture: in Judith he is a king who claims to be god (Judith 3:8; Judith 6:2), and in rabbinic legend he is the arrogant ruler par excellence. Christian writers read him in both lights, as the scourge of a sinful people and as an image of the pride that God brings low.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 27:6–8; Jeremiah 38:17–18; Daniel 4:17; Daniel 4:34–37; Judith 3:8; Judith 6:2

sections.b: Babylonian chronicles confirm his capture of Jerusalem on 2 Adar, in his seventh year (597 BC), and the appointment of a new king, which matches 2 Kings 24:10–17. Building inscriptions celebrate his work in Babylon, which echoes his boast in Daniel 4:30. No Babylonian text records a period of madness; some scholars think Daniel 4 transfers to him a tradition about the last king of Babylon, Nabonidus, who spent ten years away at Tema. Judith's "Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over the Assyrians in Nineveh" (Judith 1:1) cannot be fitted to his reign, since Nineveh fell in 612 BC; most scholars read the title as deliberate.
